content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a guideline focused on the development, attraction, recruitment, and retention of health workers in rural and remote areas. This guideline is an update to the 2010 WHO recommendations aimed at increasing access to health workers in underserved regions through improved retention strategies. The document is available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-002422-9 and 978-92-4-002423-6. It is published under a Creative Commons license, allowing non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent Creative Commons terms. If a translation of the guideline is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guideline emphasizes that WHO does not endorse any specific organizations, products, or services mentioned within the document. Additionally, any third-party materials included in the guideline require the user to obtain permission from the copyright holder for reuse. The guideline outlines key considerations for interventions aimed at addressing national priorities and meeting the expectations of health workers and rural communities. These include relevance, acceptability, feasibility, affordability, effectiveness, and impact. Indicators for measuring the long-term impact of these interventions are also discussed. The guideline is part of WHO's broader program on human resources for health. The revision process was initiated by James Campbell, Director of the Health Workforce Department at WHO, and coordinated by Michelle McIsaac, an economist in the same department. The development involved contributions from a WHO Steering Group, a Guideline Development Group, and an External Review Group, as well as input from various experts and consultants. The Steering Group facilitated the planning, identified members for the development and review groups, and contributed to drafting the guideline. The Guideline Development Group refined the scope, reviewed evidence summaries, and developed recommendations. External reviewers provided peer feedback on the draft document. The evidence review was led by Sarah Strasser from the University of Queensland, with contributions from other academic and health professionals. A systematic review of policies for recruiting and retaining health workers in underserved areas was conducted, led by Amena El-Harakeh from the American University of Beirut. A survey on stakeholder values and feasibility of increasing access to health workers in rural areas was also conducted, led by Onyema Ajuebor from WHO headquarters. The guideline introduces several key terms and concepts, including accelerated medically trained clinicians, rural attraction, availability, bundled interventions, workforce development, interprofessional education, multidisciplinary teams, recruitment, regulation, rural retention, rural training pathways, and social accountability. These terms are defined to provide clarity on the strategies and approaches discussed in the document. The production of this guideline was supported by funding from Germany, Norway, and the Universal Health Coverage (UHC) Partnership, which includes contributions from Belgium, the European Union, France, Ireland, Japan, Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, and WHO.
